title: The sky is the platter
hook: the sky is the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls: creation performs the aarti (Dhanasri M1, ang 13)
carry: you don't light it, you notice it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of hymn three, and your line: gagan mai thaal. Did you look up for one breath last night? Today, what the platter is for. Day four hundred twenty-eight.
screen: `GAGAN MAI THAAL — THE SKY, A PLATTER.`

segments.voice: Evening at a Hindu temple. The bells start. A priest lifts a brass tray with small flames burning on it and moves it in slow circles before the image of the deity. Incense curls up. Someone waves a fan of white hair. Flowers lie heaped at the front. People sing, clap, reach toward the flames and draw the warmth back over their eyes. That's an aarti. Sohila's third hymn takes the items on that tray and finds each one, much larger, somewhere in the world.
screen: `A BRASS TRAY OF FLAMES.` → `INCENSE, A FAN, FLOWERS.` → `EVERY ITEM, FOUND IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Aarti is the waving of lamps, a way of honoring what is dear by circling light before it. Now walk through the hymn with the tray in mind. The platter: the sky. The lamps: the sun and the moon. Then: taarika mandal janak moti, the circles of stars are like pearls scattered across it. More items follow, the incense, the fan, the flowers, and we'll take those tomorrow. Then the refrain. In paraphrase: what a wonderful aarti this is, O Destroyer of fear; this is Your aarti. And the unstruck sound, the music no hand plays, sounds like the temple drums. So who is performing the aarti? Not a priest. Creation itself. In the hymn, the whole universe, every evening, is lifting its lamps toward the One. In Sikh practice the hymn itself is sung as the aarti, with no tray and no flames: the sound is the offering. A few historic gurdwaras also keep an evening ceremony with lamps alongside the singing, and Sikhs differ on that practice. Both share the line's big picture: the offering is already happening, all around, all the time. You don't light it. You notice it.
screen: `AARTI: CIRCLING LIGHT IN HONOR.` · `SKY, SUN AND MOON, STARS AS PEARLS.` · `WHAT A WONDERFUL AARTI THIS IS.` · `CREATION ITSELF IS OFFERING.` · then, large: `THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the night sky. If it's dark where you are, go to a window or step outside. Find the moon if it's up, or one star, or even the orange glow of a city sky. Let your eyes rest there. Picture that sky as a tray held up in honor, and you standing underneath it as one of the people at the edge of the crowd. If it's daytime, look at the sky as it is and remember it'll be lit differently tonight. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
Aarti. The offering of circling lamps; in Sohila's third hymn, the aarti the whole creation performs, with the sky as its platter.

Your line: you don't light it, you notice it. Today, catch one ordinary thing, a streetlight, a sunset on a window, a flower by a curb, and see it as an item on the tray. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly within Kirtan Sohila, and gurdwaras also sing it on its own in the evening as the Aarti, usually without lamps, while a few historic gurdwaras also keep a lamp ceremony.

what it means: the honoring of the divine with circling lamps; in Sohila, creation itself is the one offering it.
what a scholar hears: Dhanasri M1 maps each item of the temple aarti (thaal, deepak, moti, dhoop, chavar, phool) onto sky, sun and moon, stars, breeze, wind and forests.

notes: Hymn paraphrased throughout (stars as pearls, sandalwood breeze as incense, wind as fan, forests as flowers; refrain 'what a wonderful aarti this is, O Destroyer of fear'; unstruck sound as temple drums). Confirm.
Etymology of aarti given as 'from a Sanskrit word for the waving of lamps' (aratrika/arati); confirm.
